subject: Economics
description: GDP, GNP, NNP, per-capita income, base year

questions.stem: The money value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year is the:

options.option_text: Gross National Product (GNP)
Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
Net National Product (NNP)
Per capita income

questions.explanation: GDP — production within the geographical boundaries of a country, regardless of whether the producer is domestic or foreign. GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad (NFIA). NFIA = income Indians earn abroad − income foreigners earn in India. India typically has negative NFIA (more money goes out as repatriated MNC profits than comes in via NRIs), so GNP < GDP.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Net National Product (NNP) is calculated as:

options.option_text: GNP + depreciation
GNP − depreciation
GDP + net exports
GDP − indirect taxes

questions.explanation: NNP = GNP − depreciation of capital. Depreciation represents wear and tear of existing capital used up in production. 'Net' means 'after subtracting depreciation'. NNP at factor cost = 'National Income' (the income accruing to factors of production — labour, capital, entrepreneurship). NNP at market price = NNP at factor cost + indirect taxes − subsidies.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: In India, national income statistics are compiled by the:

options.option_text: Reserve Bank of India
Central Statistics Office (NSO)
NITI Aayog
Ministry of Finance

questions.explanation: The Central Statistics Office — reorganised in 2019 as the National Statistical Office (NSO) under MoSPI (Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation) — compiles national income accounts. P. C. Mahalanobis is often called the architect of India's official statistics (he founded ISI and the NSSO). NITI Aayog is the planning think-tank (replaced the Planning Commission in 2015). RBI compiles monetary and financial statistics.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The difference between 'nominal GDP' and 'real GDP' is that:

options.option_text: Nominal is for goods, real is for services
Nominal uses current-year prices, real uses base-year prices
Nominal is for India, real is for the world
Real excludes the informal economy

questions.explanation: Nominal GDP = measured at current-year (market) prices — inflated by price changes. Real GDP = measured at constant prices of a chosen base year — strips out inflation. Real growth rate is the most widely reported measure of economic growth. The GDP deflator = (Nominal / Real) × 100 is itself an inflation measure. India's current base year is 2011-12; a revision to 2020-21 or 2022-23 is being prepared.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Per capita income of a country is calculated as:

options.option_text: GDP × population
National income ÷ total population
GDP − taxes
NNP + subsidies

questions.explanation: Per capita income = National Income / Population. Gives the average income per person per year. India's nominal per capita income was about ₹2.0 lakh in 2023-24 (approximately US$ 2,500). Rich countries often measure it at PPP (purchasing-power parity) as well — on that basis India is higher (~US$ 10,000 at PPP). Per capita income masks inequality — a Gini coefficient or decile distribution supplements it.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which method does NOT measure national income?

options.option_text: Production (Value-Added) method
Nielsen survey of consumer brand preference
Income method
Expenditure method

questions.explanation: Three equivalent approaches to national income — (i) Production / value-added method — sum of value added at each stage of output. (ii) Income method — sum of factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit). (iii) Expenditure method — sum of C + I + G + (X−M). All three must, in principle, give the same total. Consumer brand surveys are market-research tools, not national-income accounting.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The first estimate of India's national income was prepared by:

options.option_text: P. C. Mahalanobis
Dadabhai Naoroji
V. K. R. V. Rao
D. R. Gadgil

questions.explanation: Dadabhai Naoroji — 'Grand Old Man of India' — gave the first estimate of India's national income in his book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901), using it to articulate the 'Drain Theory'. The first scientific estimate came from V. K. R. V. Rao in 1931-32. Mahalanobis designed the National Income Committee (1949) and India's planning models. D. R. Gadgil was the first Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Gross National Product (GNP) differs from Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in that GNP additionally includes which of the following?

options.option_text: depreciation of capital assets within the country's territory
indirect taxes collected by the government in a fiscal year
net factor income earned from abroad by the country's residents
government transfer payments including pensions and unemployment relief

questions.explanation: GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA). When Indian residents earn wages, rent, interest, or profit abroad and those earnings are added (minus factor income paid to foreigners inside India), the result is GNP. Depreciation (option A) is subtracted from GNP to arrive at NNP — it plays no role in the GDP-to-GNP bridge. Indirect taxes (option B) distinguish market price from factor cost, which is a separate distinction unrelated to the domestic-vs-national scope.

questions.stem: Which of the following is EXCLUDED from the computation of a country's national income?

options.option_text: old-age pension payments disbursed by the government to retirees
wages paid to workers employed in the manufacturing sector
interest earned by households on fixed deposits held with banks
rent received by landlords from commercial and residential tenants

questions.explanation: Transfer payments such as old-age pensions are one-sided transactions — the government disburses money but receives no current productive service in return. National income counts only factor incomes (wages, interest, rent, profit) earned by contributing to current production. Wages (B), interest on deposits (C), and rent from property (D) are all genuine factor incomes and are therefore included.

questions.stem: Which of the following items IS included when estimating India's national income, even though no direct market transaction takes place?

options.option_text: value of unpaid household work performed by homemakers each year
black market transactions involving unregistered goods and services
lottery winnings and gambling receipts received by individuals
imputed rental value of owner-occupied residential houses each year

questions.explanation: Imputed rental value of owner-occupied houses IS included because, by convention, homeowners are treated as renting their home to themselves — a real housing service flows even without a cash transaction. Unpaid household work (A) lies outside the production boundary and is excluded despite its economic significance. Black market transactions (B) go unreported and cannot be captured. Lottery winnings (C) are transfer receipts, not factor income arising from production, so they are excluded.

questions.stem: The value-added method of measuring GDP sums up, across all producing units in the economy, which of the following?

options.option_text: the net value added at each production stage from raw material to final output
total sales revenue of all firms across every production stage combined
only the final retail price of goods sold directly to end consumers
factor payments — wages, rent, interest, and profit — across all sectors

questions.explanation: The value-added (production) method records Value Added = Output Value − Intermediate Input Cost at every stage, then sums these across all producing units. This design eliminates double counting because intermediate goods purchased from other firms are deducted. Option B (total sales revenue) would double-count intermediate goods sold between firms. Option C describes the expenditure method's final-goods logic. Option D describes the income method, which is conceptually equivalent but methodologically distinct.

questions.stem: To derive Personal Income (PI) from National Income (NI), which combination of adjustments is correct?

options.option_text: add undistributed corporate profits, then subtract transfer payments received
add corporate income tax and social security contributions paid by employers
subtract corporate tax and undistributed profits, then add transfer payments
subtract government subsidies and add all forms of household investment income

questions.explanation: PI = NI − Undistributed corporate profits − Corporate income tax − Social security contributions + Transfer payments received by households. Profits retained by firms and taxes paid by corporations never reach households, so they are subtracted; government transfers (pensions, relief) add back income households receive without producing. Option A reverses the sign on undistributed profits — these must be subtracted because they are earned within NI but never distributed to individual residents.

questions.stem: The concept of 'Green GDP' modifies conventional GDP primarily by accounting for which of the following?

options.option_text: only agricultural and forestry sector contributions to total national output
cost of environmental degradation and natural resource depletion during growth
foreign direct investment inflows and bilateral trade surplus or deficit values
informal sector output and unregistered household production value estimates

questions.explanation: Green GDP = Conventional GDP − Monetary value of environmental damage − Cost of depleting non-renewable natural resources. It measures sustainable growth by penalising output that erodes the ecological base. Option A is wrong because Green GDP applies across all sectors, not just agriculture or forestry. Option C describes adjustments relevant to cross-border factor income (GNP-type) accounting. Option D relates to the informal-economy estimation problem, which is a data-coverage issue entirely separate from environmental accounting.

questions.stem: A country's nominal GDP in the base year was ₹100 lakh crore. In the current year, nominal GDP rose to ₹130 lakh crore and the GDP deflator stood at 120 (base = 100). What is the real GDP growth rate?

options.option_text: 30 percent, since real growth equals the full rise in nominal GDP terms
20 percent, as the deflator percentage rise itself constitutes real growth
10 percent, by subtracting deflator growth (20%) from nominal growth (30%)
8.33 percent, since real GDP equals nominal GDP divided by the deflator index

questions.explanation: Real GDP = (Nominal GDP ÷ GDP Deflator) × 100 = (130 ÷ 120) × 100 = 108.33 lakh crore. Since base-year real GDP = 100 lakh crore, real growth = 8.33%. Option C (10%) applies the popular approximation rule — real growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation = 30% − 20% = 10% — which is only approximate, not exact. Option A (30%) ignores the price-level rise entirely. Option B (20%) confuses the deflator's own percentage increase with actual output growth.
